source.title: How Much Is an AI Token Worth? Scaling Laws for Wild AI-Generated Web Text
source.authors: Jenna Russell; Ben Glickenhaus; Katherine Thai; J. Wieting; M. Iyyer; Max Spero; Bradley Emi

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study runs scaling experiments on human and wild AI-generated text, finds that AI additions can reverse the loss trend seen with human-only training, and develops and evaluates a revised scaling law.
record.gate_note: Related-work results cited from other studies are not recorded. The study also reports data audits and AI-generated writing-style outcomes; these do not directly test the listed scaling-law versions and are omitted. The reported CORE outcomes are included under fits_no_version because they do not test downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains 800 nanochat models (19.9M–973M) adding wild AI text to fixed human corpora. It reports that Chinchilla holds for human-only and fresh-human data but fails when AI tokens are added, and it fits on small sizes to predict held-out larger sizes. This bears on V1, V2 and V7 in a new data setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the authors' law implies unfiltered web text at the 31.1% AI share needs 1.6× the compute of its human subset at 20 TPPh. They recommend filtering AI text, repeating human text before adding AI text, and reporting human and AI validation loss separately. The 41% error reduction is relative to the best existing law (Shukor joint).
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretraining scaling experiments and held-out loss, but varies wild AI-text additions in nanochat models rather than reproducing the original scaling experiments; fits relative changes against matched human-only controls.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported result depends on the human-token budget, AI-to-human ratio, evaluation target, and model size. The authors also state that counting the input embedding fits their laws better at the smallest sizes, and compare alternative benefit and harm forms and fitting procedures.

fits_no_version.finding: At 20 TPPh, repeating the human corpus beats adding equal AI tokens on all 18 human-text comparisons. On AI-text sets the order reverses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated human tokens are worth more than fresh AI-generated tokens for loss on human text.

fits_no_version.finding: The loss-minimising AI share is 1.0% for C4 but over 90% for Cosmopedia at 20 TPPh.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal data mixture depends on the evaluation target's provenance.

fits_no_version.finding: CORE rises about equally with AI and fresh-human additions while C4 loss moves in opposite directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark scores and human-text loss can diverge under the same data addition.

record.problems: The paper fits on models only up to 268M parameters and tests up to 973M; it studies only pretraining on English web text. The authors note that larger models may behave differently. The study uses a single nanochat architecture, and the largest extrapolation is 3.6× the largest fitted model.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model-by-budget curves and the full set of target datasets and law-comparator scores are not transcribed as separate rows; the selected rows retain the key conditions and comparisons relevant to the claim. Additional generated-text style outcomes and data-filter audit results are omitted because they do not test the listed versions.

untested.parts: Several orders of magnitude (sizes span ~1.7). Separate laws in N, D and C were not reported.
Extrapolation by orders of magnitude: the largest held-out size is 3.6× the largest fitted size. The 8B projections are untrained.
No compute-optimal N/D split is studied.
Single nanochat architecture; shape is not varied at fixed N.
No other modalities, fine-tuning or transfer. The repetition runs (6 models) fit no power law.
Downstream performance is not related to scale or loss.
Compute-optimal split and training-schedule dependence are untested.

missing.what: Fitted exponents differ by evaluation target: α from 0.12 to 0.30 and β from 0.42 to 0.96 across C4, FW22, FW26-H and Paloma.
Parameter-counting choice: counting the input embedding fits the laws better at the smallest sizes (qualitative).
On Paloma, Chinchilla's β hits its upper bound (2.5), giving a negligible data term at held-out sizes.
Absolute held-out RMSE: Chinchilla 26.93e-3 on C4 versus CD 12.51e-3 and ours 14.09e-3; the ranking differs from paired error.
The Shukor joint law fitted through 135M versus 268M projects opposite signs of the AI effect at 8B.
Chinchilla's paired error on fresh-human additions at held-out sizes is 1.32e-3.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The extrapolation ratio is small (≤3.6×), and the main metric is paired change, not absolute loss. The new law is the authors' own method, so R4 is an own-method comparison, though it does bear on V2. The R6 value was misread from the law's direction accuracy.

versions.untested_parts: The human-only scaling result is reported, but the study does not establish separate power laws in parameters, tokens, and compute across several orders of magnitude or across varied architectures.
The largest held-out models are 3.6× the largest fit size, not orders of magnitude larger; prediction of absolute loss is not the main reported metric.
The study does not optimize the parameter-count/token-count split at a fixed compute budget.
Architecture details are not varied at a fixed parameter count; all models use the nanochat architecture.
The experiments are English web-text pretraining; other modalities, repeated data as a general regime, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
CORE is measured, but the study does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with model scale or pretraining loss.
The study compares fitted laws and some fitting choices, but does not systematically vary all listed setup factors or test compute-optimal parameter/token exponents.

rows.subject: nanochat models (human-only controls; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size and human tokens per parameter in human-only runs; evaluated held-out loss.
rows.value: The paper states that models trained on only human text follow Chinchilla scaling laws.
rows.note: Aggregate statement about the human-only runs; the paper does not give a separate numerical fit result for this statement here.
rows.check: Qualitative statement only. The supporting number is Chinchilla's paired error on fresh-human additions at held-out sizes (1.32e-3 on C4, §4.1) and the Fig. 14 collapse; add it. Size range is about 1.7 orders of magnitude, not several.

rows.subject: nanochat models (aggregate across reported sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Added wild AI tokens to fixed human corpora and measured change in held-out C4 loss against each human-only control.
rows.measure: Change in C4 loss versus the human-only control
rows.value: At 5 TPPh, AI text decreases loss even at large AI budgets.
rows.note: The text summarizes the pattern across models; individual plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Bears on V7 only as loss departing from a single token-count power law. Value is a figure summary with no numbers. Fig. 12 gives up to 3.0% C4 reduction at 5 TPPh.

rows.subject: nanochat models (aggregate across reported sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Added wild AI tokens to fixed human corpora and measured change in held-out C4 loss against each human-only control.

conditions.value: AI text raises loss immediately; harm grows with added AI text

rows.measure: Change in C4 loss versus the human-only control
rows.value: For Chinchilla-optimal models (20 or more TPPh), AI text raises loss immediately, with larger increases at larger model sizes.
rows.note: Aggregate textual result; the paper reports curves by size and budget but does not state one combined numeric value.
rows.check: Same as R2. The 'AI-to-human ratio' condition field holds a result, not a condition; it should be r from 0 to 64.

rows.subject: Scaling-law fit for nanochat models; held-out 477M and 973M runs
rows.size_stated: Fit sizes up to 268M; held-out sizes 477M and 973M
rows.operation_detail: Fit the proposed law on smaller runs and predict the change in loss from AI additions on held-out larger runs.

conditions.value: 477M and 973M; 1.8× and 3.6× the largest fitted size

rows.measure: Paired RMSE of predicted versus observed change in log loss
rows.baseline: Best existing comparator: Shukor joint law, 1.41 × 10−3 on C4
rows.value: Proposed law: 0.83 × 10−3 on C4; it predicts held-out models up to 3.6× larger.
rows.uncertainty: The bootstrap gap versus Shukor joint is 0.58 × 10−3, 95% interval 0.32 to 0.84; proposed-law RMSE 95% interval 0.64 to 0.99 × 10−3.
rows.note: Predictive result is for the effect of AI additions relative to human-only controls, not a broad prediction of absolute loss orders of magnitude beyond the fit range.
rows.check: This is the study's own law compared with others. It is valid for V2 only as fit-small/predict-larger (1.8–3.6×) of the paired change, not absolute loss. Remove the V7 link. On absolute RMSE the ranking differs: CD 12.51, ATLAS 13.65, ours 14.09 (Table 10).

source_check.correct: The proposed law achieves paired log-loss-change RMSE 0.83×10−3 versus Shukor joint 1.41×10−3. Extrapolation is only 1.8× and 3.6× beyond the largest fitted model; state=cannot_determine for V2 as defined, which specifies loss prediction orders of magnitude beyond fitted runs.
source_check.problem: The numerical result is correct, but successful short-range prediction of paired changes does not establish the stated V2 effect.

rows.subject: Chinchilla law fitted/evaluated on the study's runs
rows.size_stated: Fit sizes 19.9M to 268M; held-out sizes 477M and 973M
rows.operation_detail: Benchmarked Chinchilla predictions for AI-token additions against paired held-out runs.
rows.measure: Paired RMSE of predicted versus observed change in log loss
rows.baseline: Observed paired changes in the held-out AI-addition runs
rows.note: The paper says Chinchilla predicts fresh-human additions substantially better than AI additions and poorly captures the AI-addition behavior.
rows.check: Baseline should be Chinchilla's paired error on fresh-human additions (1.32e-3), not 'observed paired changes'. Chinchilla's failure on AI additions (4.32e-3) is the V7 effect in full, so the state is observed, not partial. For V2 it shows a law fitted on small runs mispredicting larger ones.

source_check.correct: Comparison baseline: Chinchilla paired C4 error 1.32×10−3 on fresh-human additions; AI-addition error 4.32×10−3. State=observed for V7; cannot_determine for V2's orders-of-magnitude loss extrapolation.
source_check.locator_found: §4.1, reserved-size comparison; Table 1; §4.3, held-out size ratios
source_check.problem: Observed paired changes are the scoring reference, not the comparative baseline; the observed state fits V7 but does not establish V2 as written.

rows.subject: nanochat models (aggregate; filtering pairs)
rows.operation_detail: Compared training with a 22.3% AI mix against paired training on only the human subset, removing AI text without replacement.
rows.measure: Direction of held-out C4 loss change after filtering AI text
rows.baseline: Run trained with the AI-containing mix
rows.value: Filtering reduced C4 loss in 18 of 19 pairs; the paper reports lower loss for models above about 10 to 15 TPPh, less at larger sizes.
rows.uncertainty: Paired error of the proposed law: 3.28 × 10−3
rows.note: This result indicates the effect depends on human-data budget and model size.
rows.check: Value is wrong. '18 of 19' is the proposed law's direction accuracy. Filtering lowered C4 loss in 13 of 19 pairs, and Chinchilla predicted a rise in all 13. The uncertainty field (3.28e-3) is the law's error, not uncertainty of the measurement. Size is stated (Fig. 5 circles include 973M).

rows.subject: nanochat models (19.9M and 35.8M; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared repeating the human corpus with adding the same number of AI tokens at 20 TPPh.

conditions.value: 1, 4, or 8 times the human corpus in tokens

rows.measure: C4 loss difference between repeating human text and adding AI text
rows.baseline: AI-text addition at the same token amount
rows.value: After one added epoch, loss was 2.3% lower with repeated human tokens; after eight added epochs, the gap was 6.3–6.4%.
rows.note: The paper reports this as an aggregate summary; §F.3 says repetition beat AI additions in all 18 comparisons on the three human-text evaluation sets.
rows.check: Compares repetition with AI addition with no scaling fit or exponent. It does not measure fit-dependence of exponents; record under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Scaling-law fit for nanochat models
rows.size_stated: Fit on 19.9M to 268M; evaluated up to 973M
rows.operation_detail: Fit the study's law separately for each evaluation target and minimize predicted loss over AI-to-human training ratio, holding model size and human corpus fixed.
rows.value: 1.0% AI share for C4 at 20 TPPh.
rows.note: This is an optimum over AI mixture share at fixed model size and human corpus, not the compute-optimal parameter/token split in V3.
rows.check: This is an optimum derived from the study's own law, not a measured scaling result. Correctly unlinked.

rows.subject: nanochat models (AI and fresh-human additions; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared CORE score changes from adding AI tokens or the same number of fresh human tokens against each run's human-only control.

conditions.value: At 20 TPPh, at least as many tokens as the human corpus contains

rows.value: At 20 TPPh, CORE rose 1.6 points with AI text and 1.9 points with fresh human text (23 and 6 runs, respectively).
rows.locator: §G; Figure 23; “Same benchmark scores, different fit to human text”
rows.note: This does not report downstream performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss, so it does not test V6.
rows.check: CORE is not reported as a function of scale or loss. The authors say the models are too small for meaningful performance. Correctly unlinked.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Plain Chinchilla, and the Shukor joint law, extrapolating AI-addition effects
source_check.reason: The Chinchilla errors concern short-range paired-change prediction. The inconsistent 8B projections have no trained 8B result against which to check them. These findings support setup and fit dependence under V7, but do not test V2's stated extrapolation regime.

relationships.condition: Adding or removing wild AI text in pretraining data
relationships.reason: Loss is not a function of token count alone. AI tokens help at 5 TPPh and hurt from 20 TPPh (R2, R3). Chinchilla errs 3× more on AI than on human additions (R5). Removing AI text lowered loss in 13 of 19 pairs where Chinchilla predicted a rise (R6).
relationships.display_finding: AI tokens helped at 5 TPPh but hurt from 20 TPPh; Chinchilla made 3× larger errors for AI additions than human additions, and removing AI text lowered loss in 13 of 19 pairs where Chinchilla predicted an increase.
